prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock and its realization at a fractional uncertainty of about 1e-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B015 as a single-part prize to Katori and Ye. After the full first-round exchange the science looks no weaker and the attribution looks stronger. The invention is one idea with a clear owner: trapping many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength, where the lattice light shift on the clock transition cancels, so the atoms sit in the Lamb-Dicke regime without Doppler or recoil broadening. The realization is equally clear: Ye's strontium clock took that architecture to about 1e-18 systematic uncertainty, resolved the gravitational redshift over a millimetre, and had to control the many-body (collisional and Fermi-degenerate) physics that a large atom number brings. The result does not rest on one laboratory: JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and NPL agree at that level, so what is confirmed is the concept and not one apparatus. The chair asks whether the 1e-18 wording is acceptable. I now think it should be in the citation, because it is what separates this prize from the 2005 comb prize, which made optical frequencies countable, and from the 2012 ion-control prize, which concerns single quantum systems. I have therefore added it to my citation, which in round 1 did not state it. On the chair's credit question, my line between inventor and refiner is this: Katori supplied the idea that makes a many-atom optical clock possible at all, and Ye supplied the demonstration that it reaches the accuracy regime the idea promised. The Paris, PTB and NIST groups, and the single-ion clocks, showed the same architecture or a competing one working, but none of them changed what a clock is or what it can reach. On the SI second, I treat redefinition as supporting evidence only. The merit rests on performance already demonstrated and independently confirmed, and I agree with Mehlig that a prize should not wait on a metrological-body timetable.
statement.case_against: The reservations that remain are real. First, novelty against 2005 and 2012: a committee can fairly read a lattice-clock prize as a refinement of recognised precision-frequency work rather than a new step, and Kroll and Danielsson both press that the clock is an enabling instrument whose discovery content about nature (geodesy, constants, dark-matter searches) is still partly prospective. I think the invention criterion is met without that, but this is a judgment on which atomic-physics colleagues, myself included, may be biased towards the field. Second, credit at the edges: the Paris (Lemonde, Le Targat), PTB, NIST and Ludlow and Lemke work, and the ion-clock lineage, reached comparable uncertainties by other routes, and a two-name citation does not mention them. Third, B006 is the candidate that most members rank near the top, and a configuration that omits it must be justified by maturity and interpretation, not by a count. Pairing it with B015 is not feasible within the three-person limit, since Katori and Ye already use two places and the MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer triple would have to be cut to one name, which would be a worse attribution than either prize alone.

responses.point: He holds B006 first as a prediction followed by an unasked-for experimental surprise, argues that the discovery of the phases does not depend on the pairing mechanism, and asks what evidence would move him to B015.
responses.response: I accept that the observation of correlated and superconducting states does not depend on the mechanism, and that is the strongest form of his argument. My reservation is narrower: the citation would need to say what was discovered, and members who lean towards B006 (Eriksson, Mehlig, Pearce, Olsson) all hesitate on interpretation, twist-angle disorder and the omitted experimental team. I agree that the Bistritzer-MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero division of labour is neat, but he himself notes that Cao and other groups are outside it. For B015 the core claim has not changed in a decade and the answer is checked against an external reference, which is what I would point him to. I am keeping B006 as my first alternative and I would support it in a later year.

responses.point: He asks the committee to state what the lattice clock teaches us about nature, and whether a two-part prize pairing B015 with a condensed-matter candidate is worth exploring.
responses.response: On the first question, the lattice clock has already measured something: a gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale atom cloud, and bounds on drifts of constants that no earlier clock could set. That is a test of relativity, not only a precision figure, and I would not let the citation hide it. On a two-part prize, I explored it and I do not think it works. With Katori and Ye using two of the three places, the second part could carry one name, and none of the shortlisted pairings (B006, B055, B024) can be reduced to one person without damaging the attribution that makes them attractive. I would rather not weaken a clean prize to add a part.

responses.point: He now treats B015 as a first-rate invention with clean credit, but says it does not exceed B055 in scientific reach, and he defends B055 on maturity and a stable interpretation.
responses.response: I take the point on reach: topological classification changed how a whole community organises electronic structure, and a clock does not do that. But I weigh the prize criteria differently, as an invention with a demonstrated payoff and a confirmed, bounded credit. Here B055 is weaker than its reach suggests: by his own account the credit leaves out Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore, Balents, Roy and the ARPES work, and the framing question (narrow quantum spin Hall or broad topological insulators) is unresolved. A prize that must be contested on who is excluded is a worse fit for this year than one in which the supplied names match the idea and the demonstration. I do not oppose B055 for a later year with a defined citation.

responses.point: He argues that circuit QED is as mature as lattice clocks, that the 2025 prize concerned macroscopic tunnelling in a single circuit and not photon coupling and readout, and he accepts the transmon qualification.
responses.response: That distinction between the 2025 subject and circuit QED is fair, and it weakens my own timing worry, so I no longer treat 2025 as disqualifying. It is why B024 stays in my alternatives. What keeps it behind B015 for me is the credit: Girvin, Huang and the transmon sit outside Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf, and even he writes the citation narrowly to avoid that. I note his candid disclosure and his question about recusal; that is for the chair and the committee to decide and I make no claim about it. He is right that no further result would change the B024 case, so I would favour it in a later year.

responses.point: He moved to B015, would not pair it with ion clocks, and says the redefinition of the second should not be a precondition, but he admits the lattice clock is a capability rather than a new phenomenon.
responses.response: I agree on both procedural points: the ion-clock lineage relies on trapping and control methods that the 2012 prize already recognised, while the lattice clock has its own concept and its own systematic budget, so pairing would dilute the prize and exceed what the supplied credit can support. His remaining concern, that this is a capability and not a phenomenon, is answered only in part by the redshift and constants tests, and I think we should say so plainly. If the committee sees that as decisive, I would still point out that B023, his own first opening choice, has an exact-solution credit gap larger than anything in B015.

responses.point: She puts B015 first and wants the citation to name the lattice-clock invention and realization at 1e-18, not frequency metrology in general, and does not want Ye's many-body and redshift results read as a separate discovery.
responses.response: I agree with both. My revised citation follows her wording, naming the optical lattice clock and the fractional uncertainty of about 1e-18, and nothing about metrology in general. On the redshift and many-body work I agree it should be read as evidence of what the Katori concept makes possible. This is also why I keep two names and do not add a third: the Ye group's results belong to the realization half of the credit, not to an additional discovery.

responses.point: He asks for an explicit reason to credit Katori and Ye over the Paris, PTB, NIST and ion-clock groups, and wants the neutral-atom lattice and 1e-18 regime named so the prize is not read as a second comb or ion-control prize.
responses.response: My answer to the explicit request is the inventor and realizer distinction above: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is the concept all lattice clocks use, and Ye's group first showed it at the 1e-18 level with the full many-body analysis; the later Paris, PTB and NIST work and the record uncertainties of Ludlow and Lemke built on that architecture. I accept that this is a judgment on the supplied evidence and not a proof, and I have not checked every priority claim. I also record that his case for IceCube is strong on the science, and I would be content to see it considered in a later year if the committee can find a defensible three-name allocation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is a distinct step from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I judge it distinct, but a colleague could reasonably call it incremental in kind.

Whether the line between Katori and Ye on the one hand and the Paris, PTB, NIST and single-ion groups on the other will survive scrutiny; I rely on my recollection of the clock literature and have not verified every priority claim or uncertainty record.
Whether the 1e-18 wording in the citation is the best way to separate this prize from the earlier ones, or whether it ties the citation to a number that will be superseded.
How much weight colleagues will give to the pending redefinition of the SI second; I treat it as supporting evidence, not a precondition, but I do not know how others will weigh it.
statement.conflict_note: B015 is in my own subfield of atomic physics and precision spectroscopy, and I ranked it first, which I disclose so colleagues can weigh my view accordingly. My profile documents no collaboration with Katori or Ye, so I see no specific recusal for B015. For B024 I disclose my documented collaboration with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, which is not Wallraff's group, and I infer no relationship with the credited names. My documented collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund group on attosecond work does not touch any shortlisted ballot. No change since round 1.
